personality_voice.book_baseline: Umbridge's defining trait in the books is the sustained, deliberate gap between her surface presentation and her inner cruelty. Her voice is high-pitched, breathy and girlish ('hem, hem'); she speaks with excessive sweetness ('dear', 'kindly', 'I'm sure we'll be very good friends'); she smiles constantly, including a wide toad-like smile that appears precisely when she is inflicting harm. Her tone shifts are observable and meaningful: sweetness evaporates into cold bureaucratic precision when challenged, and into barely restrained rage when authority is defied. She is methodical and controlling — the repeated classroom rituals ('Good afternoon, Professor Umbridge'), the structured course aims on the blackboard, the insistence on hand-raising — all reveal someone who uses petty proceduralism as an instrument of dominance. Her cruelty is not impulsive; it is deliberate and pleasurable. She explicitly savours Trelawney's public humiliation ('Harry was revolted to see the enjoyment stretching her toadlike face'), examines Harry's bleeding hand with calm satisfaction ('Ah. Good. That ought to serve as a reminder'), and plans her Cruciatus attack with the excited manner of someone who has wanted to do it for a long time ('There was a nasty eager, excited look on her face that Harry had never seen before'). Her confession in the office — 'He never knew I ordered Dementors to go after Potter last summer... I was the one who actually did something about it' — reveals cold self-congratulation and a sense of personal mission. The books also show her insecurity: she name-drops 'Cornelius' before correcting herself to 'the Minister', she petulantly contacts Fudge when McGonagall bypasses her authority, and she screams accusations of ambition at McGonagall in a loss of composure. Her speech patterns include memorised bureaucratic language ('let us preserve what must be preserved, perfect what can be perfected and prune practices that ought to be prohibited'), falsely maternal diminutives toward children she is simultaneously harming, and an inability to modulate her language when genuinely enraged.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film captures the core of Umbridge's personality very effectively. Imelda Staunton's performance delivers the girlish high pitch, the persistent smile, the saccharine classroom rituals ('Good afternoon, Professor Umbridge'), the 'hem, hem' cough, and the sharp shift from sweetness to threat. Key line deliveries — 'Oh, you won't need any ink', 'Yes? That's right. Because you know, deep down, you deserve to be punished' — preserve her controlled, pleasurable cruelty in the detention scenes. The film also preserves her bureaucratic proceduralism through the course-aims blackboard, the wands-away instruction, and her clipboard presence during inspections. The Deathly Hallows courtroom scene captures the predatory enjoyment in her prosecution of Muggle-borns and the Patronus detail (warmth for the accusers, cold for the accused) correctly translates her self-satisfaction. Her visual presentation — pink cardigan, velvet bow, kitten plates — is faithfully reproduced in both films.
personality_voice.difference: Several layers of personality texture are absent or reduced. The books' Umbridge has a demonstrable insecurity that surfaces through her correction of 'Cornelius' to 'the Minister', her tantrum when Hogwarts' Headmaster office seals itself against her, and her near-hysteria when Marietta refuses to confirm the DA's activities. The film does not show these moments of composure cracking under institutional failure. The Cruciatus scene, which is the most explicit proof in the books of her willingness to commit illegal violence on a child while justifying it as Ministry necessity, is present in the film but abbreviated: in the books she shifts her wand around Harry's body 'apparently trying to decide where it would hurt most' before the confession about the Dementors bursts out — the confession is preserved in the film but the prior physical build-up and deliberate self-justification ('You are forcing me, Potter... I am sure the Minister will understand') are compressed. The books also show Umbridge's contempt for 'half-breeds' as a distinct and sustained trait (anti-werewolf legislation, her 'extremely dangerous half-breeds' comment in the first lesson, her treatment of Hagrid), which appears in the film but only briefly and without the legislative background that makes it a conviction rather than an insult. The four scenes excluded per the non-theatrical note include her speech to students and the Trelawney inspection scene; the Trelawney inspection in particular contained extended evidence of her cold proceduralism and calculated humiliation technique. Without it, the film's Umbridge inspection characterisation rests almost entirely on the Hagrid scene.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — sweetness-as-mask, bureaucratic sadism, physical and verbal menace beneath the girlish surface — is well established in both films with specific, observable evidence. The losses are real but constitute secondary texture: the insecurity reveals, the full range of her anti-half-breed conviction, and the fine-grained procedural cruelty of the Trelawney inspection (excluded). These do not alter recognition of the character but do reduce the depth of what is shown. Score: 20 out of 25.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Umbridge's structural function in Order of the Phoenix is multiple and interlocking: she is simultaneously the Ministry's instrument of institutional control over Hogwarts, the primary disciplinary antagonist for Harry personally (detentions, torture via quill, attempts to expel and incarcerate), the High Inquisitor who dismantles teacher autonomy and student freedom, the agent who manufactures the conditions that make the DA necessary, and the person who ultimately triggers the Ministry confrontation by pursuing Harry and Hermione into the Forest. She drives significant plot movement: she creates the Inquisitorial Squad, passes decree after decree, fires Trelawney, attempts to sack Hagrid, intercepts Harry's communications with Sirius, attempts Veritaserum interrogation, attempts the Cruciatus Curse, and is the direct cause of Harry and Hermione walking into the Forest — which leads to the centaur confrontation and Harry's decision to go to the Ministry. In Deathly Hallows she is the institutional face of Voldemort's purge of Muggle-borns, running the Muggle-Born Registration Commission with dementors present, and she possesses the Horcrux locket, which is the objective of the Ministry infiltration. Her agency is consistently active: she initiates, decides, enforces, searches, interrogates, threatens, and punishes.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In Order of the Phoenix, the film preserves Umbridge's role as Ministry enforcer, classroom oppressor, and institutional antagonist. She passes Educational Decrees (shown via montage), fires Trelawney (Entrance Hall scene preserved), attempts to interrogate Harry about Sirius, accompanies Harry and Hermione into the Forest and is taken by centaurs. In Deathly Hallows Part 1 she is present in the Atrium, runs the Muggle-Born Registration Commission courtroom, possesses the locket, and is Stunned by Harry. These are the essential plot functions and they are present.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several significant acts of agency are removed or curtailed. The film does not show Umbridge's attempt to use Veritaserum on Harry and Snape's active refusal to supply more — a scene in which both characters' agency is defined and their antagonism is vivid. The books' Umbridge attempts the Cruciatus Curse and is stopped only by Hermione's intervention; the film preserves this but with less textual preparation and without the full exchange in which Umbridge confesses to sending the Dementors — this confession does appear in the film, but it arrives with less dramatic weight because the lead-up (her wand moving across Harry's body, her self-justification speech) is compressed. The book's Umbridge also intercepts Harry's mail, attacks Hedwig, uses Willy Widdershins as an informant, deploys her network of surveillance across the school in ways that are shown in montage in the film but not as specific agentic acts. The Inquisitorial Squad scene (cut per non-theatrical note) removed her act of recruiting students as enforcers. More significantly, the books show Umbridge as the proximate cause of Fred and George's departure — she attempts to physically restrain them and they escape past her — while the film presents this as a spectacle with Umbridge reacting rather than actively pursuing. Her attempted sacking of Hagrid with Ministry Aurors during the Astronomy exam (books: she directs the assault, gives the order, fires Stunning Spells) is glimpsed in the film but Umbridge's personal command role in that scene is less visible. In Deathly Hallows, her courtroom role is partially transferred in focus: the film makes the Horcrux locket the primary visual and narrative focus of the scene rather than Umbridge's institutional brutality, and her prosecution of Mrs Cattermole receives less dialogue and buildup than in the book.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The core narrative functions — institutional oppressor, DA antagonist, communications interceptor, Ministry courtroom figure, locket holder — are present. But several specific agentic moments are removed (Veritaserum confrontation with Snape, the full Cruciatus sequence, the Hagrid night assault) or compressed to montage (the decree-passing campaign). The transfer rule applies to the Veritaserum scene: in the books Snape actively undermines Umbridge by lying about having no more Veritaserum; the film shows this scene but truncates it significantly, reducing Umbridge's agency in the interrogation and Snape's counter-agency. Score: 15 out of 20.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Umbridge's motivations are layered. At the surface level she is acting on Ministry orders — Fudge wants Hogwarts controlled and any mention of Voldemort's return suppressed. But the books establish that her motivations go beyond obedience: she personally volunteered to act when others were merely talking ('They were all bleating about silencing you somehow — discrediting you — but I was the one who actually did something about it'). She has genuine ideological convictions about blood purity (the anti-werewolf legislation, her contempt for 'half-breeds') that precede and exceed her Ministry role. She derives personal pleasure from authority and from the suffering of those she punishes — this is an internal drive, not simply professional conduct. She experiences something close to joy during Trelawney's humiliation and during Harry's detentions. Her internal conflict, such as it is, is visible in the Cruciatus scene: she shifts her weight, talks herself into it, justifies it repeatedly ('You are forcing me, Potter'), suggesting that even she recognises the line she is crossing — though she crosses it anyway. In Deathly Hallows her motivation is to advance within the new regime by demonstrating zealous enforcement of its ideology.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the Ministry-as-motivation clearly and establishes her personal investment through the detention scenes and the 'you deserve to be punished' line. Her Dementor confession preserves the personal initiative motivation. In Deathly Hallows, the courtroom scene shows her enforcing blood-purity ideology actively, and the detail of her claiming the locket as a 'family heirloom' (in the book) appears to be streamlined in the film — the locket is simply around her neck without the dialogue about Selwyn ancestry. The Patronus detail (her cat Patronus, bright because she is happy in her element) is a strong, economical translation of her self-satisfaction motivation.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The blood-purity ideology as a sustained personal conviction is underweighted in the film. In the books, the anti-werewolf legislation and her 'half-breed' contempt across multiple scenes establish this as a deep conviction; the film shows it briefly in her treatment of Hagrid and in the Muggle-Born Registration Commission but without the legislative backstory that makes it a revealed character motivation rather than incidental cruelty. The self-justification arc in the Cruciatus scene — where she works herself up and talks herself through the moral threshold — is compressed in the film. The books show her motivation for the Dementor attack as genuinely self-initiated action, and this is preserved in the film's dialogue, though the weight of the revelation is reduced by the scene's pacing.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Core motivations (Ministry enforcement, personal pleasure in authority, genuine ideological conviction) are present and recognisable. The ideology motivation is underexplained relative to the books but not absent. The self-justification texture of the Cruciatus scene is simplified but the essential motivation is intact. Score: 11 out of 15.

character_arc.book_baseline: Umbridge's arc in Order of the Phoenix is a rise-and-fall structure: she arrives as an unknown quantity, rapidly accumulates institutional power (High Inquisitor, then Headmistress), reaches her apex when Dumbledore flees and she effectively controls Hogwarts, and then collapses — her office seals against her, the school resists her en masse (Peeves, Skiving Snackboxes, Nifflers), Fred and George humiliate her publicly, the teachers passively undermine her, and she is ultimately carried away by centaurs in a scene of complete loss of control and dignity. Her return to the hospital wing — silent, unable to speak, trembling at hoof-sounds — and her final departure (chased by Peeves) completes the humiliation. In Deathly Hallows she has a smaller but coherent arc within the infiltration sequence: she is in institutional power, conducting interrogations from a position of authority, and is Stunned and stripped of the Horcrux. The arc is flat in the sense that she does not change internally — she remains what she is — but her external trajectory is a clear rise-and-fall.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film follows the same rise-and-fall structure in Order of the Phoenix: establishment, accumulation of power (decree montage), Headmistress appointment, resistance from students and staff, Forest scene and centaur removal. The Deathly Hallows arc (institutional authority → Stunned) is preserved. The post-Forest hospital wing scene, which shows the depth of her psychological collapse (the hoof-sound trigger), is present in the film.
character_arc.difference: The peak of Umbridge's power is less fully dramatised in the film than in the books. The books show her Headmistress period as a time of sustained, escalating institutional dominance — new decrees appearing daily, teachers being systematically undermined, Hagrid's attempted sacking with Aurors, the Niffler incidents, Peeves's campaign against her. The film compresses this into a montage and selected scenes, which means the depth of her reach and the scale of the resistance it provokes are both underrepresented. The specific arc beat of Hogwarts sealing its office against her (a moment of institutional rejection that is particularly humiliating given her power-accumulation arc) is mentioned in the books but not shown in the film. The hospital wing collapse is shown but briefly. These are compression losses rather than arc alterations.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The structural arc — rise, apex, collapse, humiliation — is intact and faithfully rendered in both films. The compression of the Headmistress period slightly reduces the peak of the arc, which in turn slightly reduces the impact of the fall, but the arc's shape and trajectory are correct. Score: 13 out of 15.

key_relationships.book_baseline: The books establish several key relationships. With Harry: it is a sustained, escalating personal antagonism in which she specifically targets him, uses his detentions as a method of psychological attrition, and takes evident pleasure in his suffering. The relationship is personal, not merely professional — she notes his scars with satisfaction, tries to trap him repeatedly, and he carries the physical reminder of her cruelty (the hand scars) throughout the rest of the series. With Fudge: she is his instrument but also his initiative — she acts before he asks, she contacts him directly when McGonagall bypasses her, she name-drops him in ways that reveal both dependence and a sense of personal alliance ('Cornelius just sent it'). With McGonagall: the relationship is one of sustained institutional conflict and open contempt on both sides; their confrontations (the careers meeting, the Quidditch ban, the Trelawney dismissal) are among the most vivid relationship dynamics in the book. With Dumbledore: she cannot touch him directly and is visibly diminished every time he acts — his appointment of Firenze, his response to her Trelawney dismissal, his escape — and her impotent fury in these moments is a key character beat. With teachers generally: she uses inspections as instruments of humiliation, particularly toward Trelawney and Hagrid, and is actively resisted by the rest of the staff in ways that demonstrate their collective judgment of her.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry/Umbridge relationship is well preserved through the detention scenes, the classroom confrontations, and the Forest sequence. The McGonagall/Umbridge relationship is shown in the Quidditch ban scene and the careers meeting (truncated) and the Trelawney dismissal scene. The Fudge/Umbridge relationship is established but not explored in depth — in the film Fudge is more of a principal and Umbridge more of a subordinate, whereas the books show her as genuinely self-initiating. The Dumbledore/Umbridge dynamic is present (she cannot act against him directly, he outmanoeuvres her over Trelawney and Firenze, he escapes from her office) but the sustained quality of her impotent fury around Dumbledore is underrepresented. The Hagrid/Umbridge relationship is shown in the hut scene and the Thestral lesson, which is present in the theatrical cut (unlike the Trelawney inspection, which is excluded).
key_relationships.difference: The Trelawney inspection (excluded per non-theatrical note) was the primary source of the Umbridge/Trelawney relationship dynamic, which in the books is a sustained campaign of professional humiliation across multiple inspection visits. Its removal means that the Trelawney dismissal scene in the film arrives without the gradual build-up that makes it a culmination of a relationship rather than a single event. The Umbridge/Snape relationship — in which she suspects him, questions him about his career history, and eventually tries to use him as a tool in the Veritaserum interrogation — is present in the film but significantly abbreviated; the inspection of his class and her probing questions about why Dumbledore won't appoint him (a moment of subtle cruelty toward Snape that also reveals her intelligence as an interrogator) is compressed to a brief exchange. The Fudge/Umbridge relationship loses the nuance of her self-initiative relative to him. The McGonagall/Umbridge relationship is the best-preserved of the secondary relationships, with the Quidditch ban confrontation and Trelawney dismissal scene both present.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Harry/Umbridge relationship is faithfully rendered. The McGonagall/Umbridge relationship is substantially preserved. The Trelawney/Umbridge relationship loses its gradual dimension due to the excluded inspection scene. The Snape/Umbridge and Fudge/Umbridge relationships are compressed in ways that remove important dynamic texture. Score: 7 out of 10.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Umbridge's complexity in the books derives from several sources. First, the gap between her surface and interior is maintained at a very fine grain — even small moments (her correction of 'Cornelius' to 'the Minister', her tantrum at the sealed office, her near-hysteria when Marietta refuses to cooperate) reveal insecurity beneath the authoritarian performance. Second, her blood-purity ideology is given legislative specificity (anti-werewolf legislation) that makes it a conviction rather than incidental cruelty. Third, her capacity for institutional intelligence is shown: she plants informants (Willy Widdershins), monitors communications through multiple channels (mail, fires, the school floo), uses Filch's knowledge of the school, recruits the Inquisitorial Squad, places stealth-sensing spells on her office, and ultimately identifies and exploits the weak link in the DA (Marietta). This makes her a genuinely formidable antagonist rather than simply a bully. Fourth, her relationship with pleasure is specific and disturbing: she enjoys her work. The books show her in moments of 'gloating enjoyment', 'callous pleasure', and a 'nastily eager, excited look' before the Cruciatus attempt. Fifth, her self-deception — framing her torture of a child as being 'for their own good', framing the Dementor attack as 'doing what had to be done' — adds a layer of ideological self-justification that makes her more than a simple villain. In Deathly Hallows, her claiming the Horcrux locket as a 'Selwyn family heirloom' reveals her blood-purity pretension and social climbing as additional character texture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core contradiction (sweetness/cruelty) and the pleasure-in-authority trait visibly. The detention scenes, the Trelawney dismissal, and the courtroom sequence all show her enjoying her work. Her institutional intelligence is partially shown (stealth sensing spells referenced in the film's forest sequence setup, the interception of mail referenced by Sirius). The Deathly Hallows courtroom scene with dementors and the Patronus detail preserves the ideological self-satisfaction effectively.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The Trelawney inspection sequence (excluded per non-theatrical note), which was the most extended demonstration of her precision as a bureaucratic tormentor — the clipboard notes, the impossible demands, the condescending questions calibrated to humiliate — is entirely absent from the theatrical film. This removes a layer of her professional competence and the specific pleasure she takes in systematic institutional cruelty as distinct from physical cruelty. The full Marietta sequence — in which Umbridge loses composure when her witness refuses to cooperate, physically shakes her, is restrained by Kingsley, and then has to recover her poise — is present in the books but absent from the film (the DA discovery is handled differently, with Umbridge using Bombarda Maxima on the Room of Requirement rather than an informant). This removes both a moment of vulnerability/loss of control and the specific texture of her operating through informants and procedural manipulation. The Hagrid night assault — where she personally commands Ministry Aurors in a midnight attack — is glimpsed but Umbridge's personal command role in it is not prominent in the film. The locket Selwyn dialogue from Deathly Hallows (in the book she claims it as a family heirloom) is absent from the film, removing a revealing moment of social pretension. The anti-werewolf legislation background, which explains her half-breed contempt as ideological rather than incidental, is mentioned by Sirius in the book but not in the film.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The most significant complexity losses are: (1) the Trelawney inspection material (excluded, removing her most detailed demonstration of bureaucratic precision as sadism); (2) the Marietta interrogation sequence (absent from film, removing vulnerability and a specific intelligence-based method of operation); (3) the blood-purity legislative backstory (absent, reducing her ideology from conviction to behaviour); (4) the Selwyn locket dialogue (absent, removing social pretension detail). Together these constitute a noticeable simplification: the film's Umbridge is recognisably the same character but without the full texture of her institutional intelligence, her specific ideological architecture, and her moments of composure-cracking failure. Score: 9 out of 15.

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score not above 75 if a core book function, decision, or act of agency is transferred or removed) — applied: the Marietta informant sequence, which is Umbridge's most sustained exercise of intelligence-based agency in the books, is entirely absent from the film (replaced by Bombarda Maxima on the Room of Requirement wall); the Trelawney inspection is excluded; the Veritaserum interrogation scene is significantly compressed. These collectively constitute removal of core agentic functions. Total held at 75.
comparative.key_observations: The film adaptation of Umbridge is substantially faithful — the core character (sweetness-as-mask, bureaucratic sadism, institutional cruelty, pleasure in authority, blood-purity ideology) is well preserved and Imelda Staunton's performance carries the personality with high fidelity. The detention scenes, the Trelawney dismissal, the Forest sequence, and the Deathly Hallows courtroom are all effective translations. The losses are real but concentrated in specific areas: the excluded Trelawney inspection removes her most precise demonstration of professional sadism; the absent Marietta sequence removes her most complex exercise of institutional intelligence; and the blood-purity ideology loses its legislative specificity. The result is a character who is fully recognisable and effectively menacing, but slightly simplified — the film's Umbridge is a bully who enjoys power, while the book's Umbridge is additionally a competent, ideologically motivated institutional operator who uses procedure itself as an instrument of cruelty. The total of 75 reflects this: faithful in the essentials, reduced in the texture that made her one of the most precisely drawn antagonists in the series.
